Article Title: Inside science's 'forbidden experiment': Why scientists kill 9 million sea lampreys every year in the Great Lakes of America
Article Text:
Arrival of sea lampreys

Once the Welland Canal was modified by the mid-1900s, allowing ships to circumnavigate Niagara Falls, the sea lamprey population boomed

Loss of native fish

Sea lamprey feeding on a trout; fish with a wound caused by a lamprey

The forbidden experiment

More moonshots needed?

Other species like the quagga mussel and zebra mussel are now plaguing the lakes.

At the June meet-and-greet organised by the GLFC, half a dozen sea lampreys posed for the cameras at the Capitol. One of them even sucked on the palm of Representative Bill Huizenga, as per a CNN report. Among the few things the entire Congress agrees on, this is one: the invasive sea lampreys must go.For the American coasts that thrive on their seafood population, the invasive species, also known as 'vampire' fishes or the 'vampire' of the Great Lakes, has had a devastating impact on the lakes' trout, salmon and whitefish population. And thus, have inspired what scientists often call the 'forbidden experiment'.Sea Lampreys were once native to the Atlantic Ocean. The first ones arrived in Lake Ontario in the 1800s, making their way from the Atlantic Ocean, through the Hudson River, following the Erie Canal. They remained in Lake Ontario for over a century because Niagara Falls barred them from moving any further.Once the Welland Canal was modified by the mid-1900s, allowing ships to circumnavigate Niagara Falls, the sea lamprey population boomed.They had finally gained access to the upper Great Lakes. Suddenly, lampreys had more space, found more food and colonised more spawning grounds. The invasion had begun.A sea lamprey has no jaw, no proper teeth and no bones. Yet this predator can attack like a suction cup to a fish 100 times its size, using its tongue to bore a hole into its side, liquefy its tissues and feed on it. Sea lampreys are quite fertile (like other invasive species) and have a unique life cycle, for a fish. One lamprey consumes around 40 pounds of fish in 12-18 months and a female can lay 40,000-67,000 eggs, and they do it in almost every stream and river that drains into the Great Lakes. Those eggs hatch into larvae, called ammocoetes, which are eyeless, worm-like creatures that burrow in the sediment, making it impossible for predators to find them. The ammocoetes live like this for many years, feeding on algae and decomposing matter, until they are big enough to transform into the sucking predator.A single lamprey can kill up to 20 kilograms of fish in just two years. On this fishy, bloody diet, a young lamprey weighing five grams will grow 40 to 50 times larger by the time it becomes an adult. And there are thousands of these vampire fish in the Great Lakes.When the lamprey invaded the Great Lakes, lake trout, their preferred food and once a top predator fish, began dying out. By the mid-1960s, the lake trout harvest in the Great Lakes had declined to less than 200,000 kilograms per year from eight million kilograms per year in the 1920s.Alewives, small fish that lake trout ate, were no longer preyed upon. They became so abundant that every year there were massive die-offs in the lakes, and millions of dead fish would wash out on the beaches.In 1954, Canada and the United States established a partnership to tackle the sea lamprey problem, and the Great Lakes Fishery Commission (GLFC) came to be. A moonshot project to control the population succeeded in 1957, when a chemical compound called TFM (3-trifluoromethyl-4-nitrophenol) was developed, which kills lamprey larvae, without harming most native fish. Since then, “lampricide” has been applied from spring to fall to spawning areas in lake tributaries, killing young lampreys before they can enter the lakes, beyond the reach of scientists.Lampricide works because the larvae are unable to metabolise the compound, which disrupts their energy production, resulting in death. Nearly 70 years after its introduction, there’s no sign that lampreys have developed any resistance to it.Almost seven decades after the moonshot, all the effort was nearly undone. During lockdown in 2020 and 2021, the staff had to maintain social distance, which led to fewer treatments taking place and the commission was unable to implement its full control program. The lamprey population “skyrocketed” by 300% in some areas, said Greg McClinchley, director of policy and legislative affairs at the Great Lakes Fishery Commission (GLFC). “It did make (our) case.”“We call it ‘the forbidden experiment’ here in the office,” he added. “We have always said that if we don’t keep controlling sea lamprey that they will bounce back — they’re a coiled menace. But we never dared to do (it).”Around 9 million sea lampreys need to be killed every year just to prevent a population explosion. If left uncontrolled, the estimated lampreys could collapse the Great Lakes' fish stocks and with it, a multibillion-dollar fishing industry, in just five years, says the GLFC.Sea lampreys are only one of the 186 invasive species among the 3,000 species in the Great Lakes. Other species like the quagga mussel and zebra mussel are now plaguing the lakes. The mussels arrived in ballast water from commercial vessels in the 1980s, and since then have impacted the survival of fish eggs, caused toxic algae blooms, and outcompeted native mussels. Invasive mussels are also a suspected factor in the rise of avian botulism die-offs in recent decades. They concentrate botulism, and another invasive species, the round goby, eats the mussels. Scientists have theorised that poisoned gobies become paralysed and easy prey for birds, which then die from the toxin. There is currently no way to safely eliminate them from the Great Lakes.“They strip the nutrients and plankton out of the water column and collapse the food web that whitefish and other species depend on. In Lake Huron, the whitefish decline has tracked almost in lockstep with the rise in mussel biomass,” said Vito Figliomeni, executive director of the Ontario Commercial Fisheries’ Association.As per a CNN report, legislation is before Congress that would task the commission with finding a control. The bipartisan bill, dubbed the “Save Great Lakes Fish Act of 2025,” proposes a $500 million budget spread across 10 years to find a solution.
Article Summary: Sea lampreys were once native to the Atlantic Ocean. First arrived in Lake Ontario in the 1800s, making their way through the Hudson River, following the Erie Canal. Once the Welland Canal was modified by the mid-1900s, the sea lamprey population boomed.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang donates $75 million to preserve the California College of the Arts' legacy as Vanderbilt launches a new college of art, architecture and design
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's $75 million donation becomes the largest university gift of his career

Why the California College of the Arts is closing

Vanderbilt's vision for a new creative college

Preserving the California College of the Arts' legacy



Jensen Huang's vision for the future of creativity

Building on years of support for arts education



What the announcement means for San Francisco's creative community

A new chapter for creative education

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, have pledged a $75 million matching gift to Vanderbilt University to establish a new college of art, architecture and design in San Francisco while preserving the legacy of the California College of the Arts (CCA). The donation, announced through the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, is the largest university gift the couple has made to date. It comes as Vanderbilt prepares to take over CCA's campus after the renowned art school announced it would close following the 2026–27 academic year. The investment will support a new institution that blends studio-based arts education with architecture, design, technology and innovation, while ensuring key elements of CCA's artistic heritage continue for future generations.The Huangs' $75 million contribution marks the biggest university donation of Jensen Huang's philanthropic career and signals his growing interest in shaping the future of education beyond engineering and computer science. The gift is structured as a matching donation, meaning Vanderbilt must raise another $75 million before receiving the full amount. The fundraising effort has already gained strong momentum, with more than $100 million committed and over 40% of the matching target secured.The project also reflects Huang's broader philosophy that creativity, design and technology should evolve together to solve tomorrow's challenges.Founded in 1907, the California College of the Arts has educated generations of influential artists, architects, designers and creative thinkers. Alumni have gone on to shape industries ranging from fine art and industrial design to animation, fashion and architecture. Despite its global reputation, the institution struggled with declining enrolment, rising operating costs and financial pressures that intensified after the COVID-19 pandemic. Its closure after the 2026–27 academic year represents one of the most significant losses for independent arts education in the United States, highlighting the growing economic challenges faced by specialist creative institutions.Rather than simply occupying CCA's former campus, Vanderbilt intends to create a multidisciplinary institution designed for the future of creative education. The Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design will combine traditional studio practice with emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, digital design, advanced manufacturing and interdisciplinary research. Undergraduate and graduate students will work alongside engineers, entrepreneurs and scientists, reflecting the growing demand for professionals who can combine artistic imagination with technological expertise. The university believes this model will prepare graduates for careers that increasingly cross the boundaries between art, business and innovation.While CCA will cease operating as an independent institution, Vanderbilt says the school's identity will not simply disappear. The university plans to establish the California College of the Arts Institute at Vanderbilt University, dedicated to preserving the college's artistic philosophy, archives and cultural contributions. The institute will continue operating the Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts, expand artist residencies and fellowships, preserve historical collections and support research into contemporary creative practice. Vanderbilt hopes these initiatives will ensure that CCA's influence continues to inspire artists and designers long after the institution itself has closed.For Huang, the donation is about more than constructing new academic buildings. He has repeatedly argued that technological progress alone cannot solve humanity's biggest challenges without imagination, artistic thinking and human-centred design. Announcing the gift, Huang said technology expands what people can build, but art and design determine why those creations matter. He believes the most meaningful innovations emerge when artists, architects, engineers and scientists collaborate, making creative education increasingly important in an era defined by artificial intelligence and rapid technological change.The latest donation builds on the Huangs' earlier efforts to support the California College of the Arts during one of the most difficult periods in its history. In 2025, they pledged a $22.5 million matching gift aimed at helping CCA stabilise its finances and explore long-term solutions. Although the institution ultimately could not avoid closure, that funding gave university leaders valuable time to pursue alternatives, eventually leading to Vanderbilt's acquisition of the campus. Together, the Huangs have now committed $97.5 million towards preserving CCA's legacy and supporting its transition into a new chapter.The creation of Vanderbilt's new college is expected to have a lasting impact on San Francisco's cultural and innovation landscape. The city has long been recognised as a global technology hub, but it has also experienced the closure of several arts organisations because of rising costs and changing economic conditions. Supporters believe Vanderbilt's investment could strengthen the city's creative ecosystem by attracting students, artists, researchers and entrepreneurs from around the world. They also see an opportunity to build stronger partnerships between universities, museums, cultural institutions and the technology sector.The transition from the California College of the Arts to Vanderbilt's new institution represents more than the replacement of one university with another. It reflects a broader transformation in how creative education is evolving around the world. As technology becomes deeply integrated into every creative profession, universities are increasingly looking for ways to combine artistic excellence with scientific research and innovation. Backed by Jensen Huang's record-breaking donation, Vanderbilt hopes to create a college that honours CCA's remarkable legacy while preparing future generations of artists, architects and designers for a rapidly changing world.
Article Summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, have pledged a $75 million matching gift to Vanderbilt University to establish a new college of art, architecture and design in San Francisco. The donation, announced through the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, is the largest university gift the couple has made to date. It comes as Vanderbilt prepares to take over CCA's campus after the renowned art school announced it would close following the 2026–27 academic year.

Article Title: Indian diplomats at UN mission still displaced three weeks after building evacuation
Article Text:
Indian diplomats at the permanent mission of India to the UN are still displaced from their premises

NEW YORK: Indian diplomats at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN are still displaced from their premises three weeks after evacuation orders were issued for them after structural damage was reported in a high-rise under-construction building.The building of the Permanent Mission of India to the United Nations, located just over a block away from the UN headquarters, houses the Mission offices as well as residences for Indian diplomats and officers posted to the Indian mission to the UN and their families.On July 7, the entire building was evacuated, along with other high-rises and businesses in the area, after structural issues were reported in the erstwhile headquarters of pharmaceutical giant Pfizer, a 37-story high-rise, "active construction" site between Second and Third Avenues on 42nd Street in Manhattan.The Permanent Mission of India to the UN is located just across the street from the troubled high-rise. There are several UN missions, UN agency officers, prominent hotels and restaurants, residences and businesses in the area.All Indian diplomats and their families followed necessary precautions in the wake of the evacuation orders and had vacated the premises. The officers and their families had to find temporary lodging in hotels across the city.Within one day, evacuation orders for almost the entire area in the vicinity of the Pfizer building were lifted, and people moved back into their residences and office buildings. Streets in and around the impacted building too were opened for pedestrian and vehicular traffic.However, the Indian mission, a school and a hotel in the area are still under evacuation orders and cannot be accessed.Three weeks into the incident, there is still no clarity from the New York City Mayor's office or the Department of Buildings as to when the premises of the Indian mission to the UN will reopen for the officers and their families to move back in.The prolonged displacement has caused an immense amount of disruption and inconvenience to the Indian diplomats and their families.The Indian diplomats continue to fulfil their work and duties amid these disruptions, including managing the visit of External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar to the UN on July 13 to launch India's official campaign for the 2028-29 non-permanent UN Security Council seat.That high-level visit also came amid the dislocation and as the Indian mission premises remained inaccessible for its diplomats.Sources have told PTI that the difficulties faced by the Indian mission have been raised with the relevant authorities as diplomats in the Indian Permanent Mission continue to perform their work.PTI reached out to officials at the New York City Mayor's Office Department of Buildings about the status of the Indian mission building, disruption caused by the displacement now in its third week, and whether there is a timeline by which the building can be accessed again by officers and their families. There has been no response from the department.The Permanent Mission of India in New York is premised in a 27-story red granite-clad building built in 1993. The building was designed by Indian architect Charles Correa and is located between 43rd and 44th Street just off Second Avenue.New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani had described the situation at the Pfizer building as "extremely serious" and had said that the building remained unstable.NYC Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani has said in a video posted on X on July 18 that the agency had still not detected any movement in the impacted building for more than a week.While he gave an update on the measures being taken to secure the building, there has been no update from the Department or the Mayor's office as to when the premises of the Indian mission to the UN can be accessed again.
Article Summary: Indian diplomats at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN are still displaced from their premises three weeks after evacuation orders were issued for them. The building houses the Mission offices as well as residences for Indian diplomats and officers posted to the Indian mission and their families. On July 7, the entire building was evacuated, along with other high-rises and businesses in the area.

Article Title: US probing Harvard over financial aid programmes
Article Text:
US probing Harvard

WASHINGTON: The US department of justice (DoJ) said on Monday it launched a probe reviewing whether some Harvard University financial aid programmes were discriminatory. The probe is to determine whether its China-based financial aid programmes and practices exclude American-citizen students, the department said.Harvard said on Monday it "does not unlawfully discriminate on the basis of race, ethnicity, or national origin in allocating financial aid". A university spokesperson said the Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Ivy League school was reviewing the DOJ's latest letter to Harvard and would engage with govt on the topic.US law requires universities to report donations from foreign sources exceeding $250,000 in a year. Harvard has previously said it has filed reports for decades "as part of its compliance with the law."The school has also previously cast Trump administration probes as "retaliatory actions against Harvard for its refusal to surrender our independence and constitutional rights." A deal to resolve the Trump administration's broader probes against Harvard remains elusive.The Trump administration has targeted universities with probes and funding suspension threats over a range of issues. These include pro-Palestinian protests against Israel's assault on Gaza, transgender policies and climate programmes. Last month, a judge blocked the Trump administration from implementing a plan to bar foreign nationals from entering the US to study at Harvard.(This is a Reuters story)
Article Summary: The probe is to determine whether its China-based financial aid programmes and practices exclude American-citizen students. Harvard says it "does not unlawfully discriminate on the basis of race, ethnicity, or national origin in allocating financial aid" US law requires universities to report donations from foreign sources exceeding $250,000 in a year.

Article Title: Hacker breaches S Korean database of nearly all diplomats
Article Text:
10,000 records of current and retired diplomats is believed to have been compromised

A system that held roughly 10,000 records of current and retired diplomats is believed to have been compromised by an unidentified hacker, foreign ministry spokesperson Park II told reporters on Tuesday. Park didn't confirm how many records had been accessed, but Yonhap News Agency reported that no sensitive data such as identification numbers, mobile phone numbers or home addresses appeared to have been affected."It appears that a significant amount of data has been leaked," Park said. "Govt is not ruling out any possibilities, including hacking organisations behind the scenes involving other countries."The ministry was notified by a relevant govt agency in early Feb about suspicious access to the online education system at the academy, Yonhap reported. The ministry shut down the system, which has remained offline since while an investigation is under way.South Korea is still reeling from a string of cybersecurity incidents, including a high-profile breach of Coupang, its leading online retailer. Last year, regulators discovered that a former employee improperly accessed personal information from nearly 34 million accounts, or about two-thirds of the country's population.North Korean hackers have carried out a series of cyberattacks in recent years, including the largest digital heist in the history of cryptocurrency in Feb last year.(This is a Bloomberg story)
Article Summary: A system that held roughly 10,000 records of current and retired diplomats is believed to have been compromised by an unidentified hacker. South Korea is still reeling from a string of cybersecurity incidents, including a high-profile breach of Coupang, its leading online retailer.

Article Title: Trump admin can't strip immigrants of work permits: Federal judge
Article Text:
US district judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston sided with a coalition of immigrant rights groups

(This is a Reuters story)

BOSTON: A federal judge Tuesday temporarily blocked Trump administration from stripping thousands of asylum seekers and immigrants who have 'Temporary Protected Status' (TPS) of their ability to work in the US.US district judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston sided with a coalition of immigrant rights groups and labour unions that sued to block US citizenship and immigration services (USCIS) from moving forward with a series of policies designed to implement new immigration-related restrictions enacted by Congress last year.Gorton's order will be in place until he decides whether to issue a longer-term pause of the Trump administration's policy. The judge said he would rule on that by Aug 5. USCIS did not respond to a request for comment. Trump's signature tax and spending law that was passed by the Congress in 2025 for the first time imposed fees to apply for asylum and restricted employment authorisation for people with TPS.
Article Summary: US district judge Nathaniel Gorton in Boston sided with a coalition of immigrant rights groups and labour unions. The judge said he would rule on that by Aug 5. Trump's signature tax and spending law that was passed by the Congress in 2025 for the first time imposed fees to apply for asylum.

Article Title: US airlines to resume direct flights to Lebanon after 40 years, says Donald Trump
Article Text:
Trump speaks during a meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in the Oval Office at White House

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday announced that American airlines will be allowed to resume direct flights to Lebanon for the first time in more than four decades, following talks with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House.The announcement came shortly after the two leaders concluded their meeting, during which they discussed efforts to maintain stability in Lebanon after months of conflict between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah group, as well as ways to strengthen bilateral ties."I am hereby directing my Administration to allow all US airline carriers to fly directly to Lebanon so that Americans can easily visit this beautiful land," Trump said in a post on social media after Aoun left the White House.Direct commercial flights between the United States and Lebanon have been suspended since 1985, when the Reagan administration halted the route following the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.While announcing the move, Trump also pledged continued US support for Lebanon, describing the country as one that had been unfairly treated."It's been a very badly treated place and country, and we're going to have it properly treated and treated with the respect it deserves.We're gonna help it a lot," Trump said during his meeting with Aoun, without outlining specific measures.However, despite the administration's decision, it remains uncertain when direct services will actually resume. The ongoing conflict involving Iran, broader regional airspace disruptions and lingering security concerns linked to Hezbollah's influence in parts of Lebanon are expected to make airlines cautious about restarting operations.Aoun's four-day visit to Washington also focused on securing long-term stability in southern Lebanon and strengthening cooperation with the United States amid continuing regional tensions.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump announced that American airlines will be allowed to resume direct flights to Lebanon for the first time in more than four decades. Direct commercial flights between the United States and Lebanon have been suspended since 1985. The Reagan administration halted the route following the hijacking of TWA Flight 847.

Article Title: James Patten sentenced to 21 months in prison over $100 million New Jersey deli stock fraud
Article Text:
James Patten sentenced to 21 months in prison over $100 million New Jersey deli stock fraud (Photo: Dan Mangan | CNBC)

Judge cites repeat fraud conviction

How a small deli became a $100 million company

Scheme began years before investigation

Investigation helped expose the case

James Patten, the former stockbroker behind the infamous stock manipulation scheme that turned a small, money-losing New Jersey deli into a company valued at nearly $100 million, has been sentenced to 21 months in federal prison.Patten, 67, was sentenced on Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Christine O'Hearn in Camden, New Jersey, bringing one of Wall Street's most unusual securities fraud cases to a close. According to CNBC, Patten had asked the court to spare him prison, but the judge rejected the request, citing his prior fraud conviction and repeated criminal conduct."This is his idea," Judge O'Hearn said while handing down the sentence, noting that Patten launched the scheme while still on supervised release from an earlier federal fraud conviction.The North Carolina resident had previously served 27 months in prison in another federal fraud case and still owed restitution when he became involved in the deli stock manipulation scheme.In addition to the 21-month prison sentence, Patten was ordered to serve three years of supervised release and pay approximately $5 million in restitution.Before sentencing, Patten apologized to the court."I stand today before you to apologize, to take full responsibility for my actions," he said, becoming emotional as he apologized to his family and young wrestlers he had coached."There is no excuse," Patten added.After leaving court, he declined further comment.Patten and his co-conspirators, Peter Coker Sr. and Peter Coker Jr., admitted to manipulating the share prices of Hometown International, which owned Your Hometown Deli in Paulsboro, New Jersey, and another shell company called E-Waste.Prosecutors said the scheme artificially inflated Hometown International's stock price by 939% and E-Waste's by nearly 19,900%.The inflated valuations were intended to make the companies attractive for reverse mergers, allowing private businesses to go public through the shell companies.Despite owning little more than a neighborhood deli that was losing money, Hometown International's market capitalization soared to around $100 million, drawing widespread attention on Wall Street.According to prosecutors, Patten first suggested creating Hometown International in 2014 after learning that his former high school wrestling teammate Paul Morina and another individual planned to open a deli in Paulsboro.Authorities said Morina, a respected high school principal and wrestling coach, and the deli's co-owner were unaware of Patten's plan to manipulate the company's shares.Patten became the last of the three defendants in the case to be sentenced. Peter Coker Sr. received a six-month prison sentence, while Peter Coker Jr. was sentenced to 40 months.Federal charges against Patten and the Cokers were filed in September 2022, more than a year after CNBC published an investigation detailing unusual links between Hometown International, E-Waste, Patten's prior legal troubles and consulting arrangements involving the companies.The story gained national attention after hedge fund manager David Einhorn highlighted the company's extraordinary valuation in a 2021 investor letter."The pastrami must be amazing," Einhorn famously wrote, mocking the fact that a single, struggling deli had somehow become a company worth nearly $100 million.Your Hometown Deli closed in 2022, but the case remains one of the most bizarre examples of stock market manipulation in recent years.
Article Summary: James Patten, 67, was sentenced to 21 months in federal prison. Patten and two co-conspirators manipulated the share prices of Hometown International, which owned Your Hometown Deli in Paulsboro, New Jersey. The company's market capitalization soared to around $100 million.

Article Title: An 11-year-old boy is bringing storytime to shelter animals, reading to dogs and cats so they feel calmer while waiting for forever homes
Article Text:
Nehemiah had been working towards the 100-hour milestone since joining the programme. (Picture: JHS)

First visit to 100 hours

Shelter praises Nehemiah

An 11-year-old boy in Florida has completed more than 100 hours of reading to rescue animals at a local shelter, becoming the first child to achieve the milestone through the Jacksonville Humane Society’s Pawsitive Reading programme.Nehemiah Turner started volunteering at the Jacksonville Humane Society (JHS) in 2024. For the past two years, he has spent time reading books to dogs and cats waiting for adoption. With support from his grandmother, Nehemiah continued his visits until he completed his goal of 100 hours.According to People's magazine, the young volunteer enjoys spending time with the animals and hopes his reading helps them feel calmer while they wait for new homes.The Jacksonville Humane Society’s Pawsitive Reading programme allows children to visit the shelter and read aloud to pets. The programme is designed to provide enrichment for both children and animals.According to JHS, simply listening to a person read aloud can help lower stress levels in animals. The programme also helps children improve their reading skills in a safe and friendly environment.Nehemiah had been working towards the 100-hour milestone since joining the programme.JHS said participants earn paw print stickers on their name badges as they complete reading hour milestones, with a gold paw print sticker being the highest achievement.After reaching 100 hours, Nehemiah received a certificate from the shelter recognising his achievement. Photos shared by JHS showed the 11-year-old sitting near dogs’ living areas and reading books to the animals. He was also seen holding his certificate celebrating his volunteer service.ID@undefinedCaption not available.ID@undefinedCaption not available.ID@undefinedCaption not available.ID@undefinedCaption not available.Nehemiah described his experience of reading to animals as calming. “It’s soothing, feels good, calm. They’re comforted animals, not like a whole bunch of barking is happening,” he told Action News Jax.One dog that became especially close to Nehemiah was Hopper. The Jacksonville Humane Society said he read to Hopper during every visit until the dog found a home after spending nearly 400 days at the shelter.The shelter said his dedication has created a positive impact beyond the animals he reads to. Jacksonville Humane Society CEO Lawrence Nicolas praised Nehemiah’s commitment to helping homeless animals.“Nehemiah’s story perfectly embodies our core belief at the Jacksonville Humane Society that generosity breeds joy,” Nicolas said.“In a world where we’ve become increasingly reliant on screens, here is a young man who quietly set a goal to help homeless animals by reading books and, in doing so, has inspired his entire community,” he added.Nicolas said the organisation is proud of Nehemiah and grateful for the contribution made by him and other children participating in the Pawsitive Reading programme.The Pawsitive Reading programme at Jacksonville Humane Society is open to children who want to spend time reading with shelter animals. Before joining, children and a parent or guardian must attend a one-time orientation session.After completing the orientation, participants can visit the shelter during opening hours to read to dogs and cats. Children are encouraged to spend at least 30 minutes reading during each visit, with no maximum time limit.Participants can bring their own books or choose from the shelter’s Pawsitive Reading library. The programme also provides children with an opportunity to practise reading in a comfortable environment while spending time with animals.
Article Summary: Nehemiah Turner started volunteering at the Jacksonville Humane Society in 2024. For the past two years, he has spent time reading books to dogs and cats waiting for adoption. With support from his grandmother, Nehemiah continued his visits until he completed his goal of 100 hours. He hopes his reading helps them feel calmer while they wait for new homes.

Article Title: 'Are you the only Indian hire?' AI engineer denied B1 visa for company offsite, Redditors point out he has to prove why the meeting can't be held online
Article Text:
Indian AI engineer shares visa denial experience for company offsite in the US.

Getting a US visa for travel and business purposes has become extremely tricky as visa officers reject applications if they even have the slightest doubt that the applicant may not come back to their home country country; or start looking for a job in the US.An AI engineer shared his experience of B1 visa denial at the Delhi consulate on Reddit , as he gave his background that he works for a US-based startup from India. But his payroll and employment is through another company. The company's offsite is in October, for which he applied for a visa and got rejected. The Redditor shared how the conversation went.Officer: What's your job title?Redditor: AI Engineer.Officer: Where do you work?Redditor: I work for Company A. My employment in India is through Company B, which handles my payroll.Officer: Why do you need to go to the US? What do you do?Redditor: I'm an AI Engineer working on AI workflow automation software. This trip is for our engineering offsite. During the meeting, we'll discuss business priorities for the next quarter, and since I'm one of the early/core engineering team members, I'm required to participate in engineering planning and technical decisions.Officer: So it's your own business?Redditor: No, I'm an employee.Officer: How long have you been with the company?Redditor: Since September last year.Officer: Are you the only Indian hire?Redditor: Yes.Officer: And you're the only one traveling?Redditor: Yes. I'm the only employee traveling from India. We're a remote company with employees in other countries like Mexico and Canada, so team members from those locations will also be attending.After this conversation, the man was handed a 214(b) refusal slip, which means the applicant does not have enough ties to his home country, but the man said that he was never asked about his family members and he could have proved that he has his mother, wife and a property under his name in India.Redditors pointed out that since he works for a US company, it raises a red flag for visa officers, as he could not prove why he needed to attend the offsite, as the meeting can also be held online. Some Redditors opined that there is nothing he could do better next time he applies as visa approval mostly depends on the officer and another officer may have approved his visa.
Article Summary: An AI engineer shared his experience of B1 visa denial at the Delhi consulate on Reddit. He gave his background that he works for a US-based startup from India. The company's offsite is in October, for which he applied for a visa and got rejected.

Article Title: Gates Foundation finds no evidence of wrongdoing in Epstein review, approves new governance measures
Article Text:
Gates Foundation concludes external review of engagement with Epstein

Board approves governance reforms

Creating a centralised vetting process for brokers, donor advisors and individuals who facilitate funding partnerships connected to the foundation through the Chair, Governing Board or Executive Leadership Team.

Establishing an escalation process for organisational risks on projects introduced by senior leadership

Clarifying roles for personnel who hold dual roles with the foundation and other entities associated with the Chair

Enhancing policies addressing conflicts of interest and the handling of sensitive foundation records

'Trust and transparency are never compromised'

The Gates Foundation has concluded its external review of its past engagements with Jeffrey Epstein , finding no evidence of wrongdoing while approving new governance measures.The review, conducted by law firm WilmerHale and commissioned by CEO Mark Suzman in March, found no evidence that Epstein was paid by the foundation or that staff had knowledge of his criminal activities. It confirmed the foundation's primary engagement with Epstein from 2011-2014 involved a proposed donor advised fund that was abandoned and grant funding to the International Peace Institute for polio eradication.The foundation's Governing Board unanimously approved new vetting and governance measures, including centralized vetting of brokers and donor advisors, an escalation process for organizational risks, enhanced conflict-of-interest policies, and stronger procedures for handling sensitive records."The review found no evidence that Epstein was paid by the foundation," the foundation said in a statement. "It also found no evidence of participation in, or knowledge of, Epstein's ongoing sex trafficking operations or criminal activities."Earlier this year, the foundation acknowledged that it regretted having any employees interact with Epstein in any way.The foundation's Governing Board unanimously approved a series of actions to strengthen internal processes going forward:"The work we do depends on integrity and earning and maintaining the trust of partners," Suzman said."That's why we welcome the findings of this external review and are moving forward with Board-approved actions to further strengthen how we vet partners, manage risk and ensure accountability going forward."Bill Gates said: "Completing this review is an important step in providing the clarity that partners, employees, and grantees deserve as well as strengthening our oversight with additional policies going forward. The work the foundation does to save lives and unlock opportunities so people everywhere can lead healthier, more productive lives, is more important than ever. We are committed to ensuring trust and transparency are never compromised. "Board member Tom Tierney said: "The review prompted hard questions and we got straight answers. The trust of employees, partners, and the communities the foundation serves is fundamental to its mission."Earlier this year, the foundation acknowledged that it regretted having any employees interact with Epstein in any way. In March, CEO Mark Suzman commissioned the external review with the support of Gates and the independent Governing Board members.
Article Summary: The Gates Foundation has concluded its external review of its past engagements with Jeffrey Epstein. The review found no evidence of wrongdoing while approving new governance measures. The foundation's Governing Board unanimously approved new vetting and governance measures, including centralized vetting of brokers and donor advisors.

Article Title: Illegal immigrant who murdered girlfriend sues Trump over campaign ad; seeks $75 million and US citizenship
Article Text:
Brandon Ortiz-Vite is serving 39–102 years for killing girlfriend Ruby Garcia.

An illegal immigrant serving a decades-long prison sentence for murdering his girlfriend has filed a federal lawsuit against US President Donald Trump, seeking $75 million in damages, a public apology, and even US citizenship, claiming the president unfairly turned him into a political symbol during the 2024 election campaign.Brandon Ortiz-Vite, 27, a Mexican national, is serving 39 to 102 years in prison after pleading guilty to the 2024 killing of his girlfriend, Ruby Garcia, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, Fox News reported.Garcia was shot multiple times following an argument, and her body was left on the side of a road. Ortiz-Vite surrendered to police two days later and admitted to the killing.In a handwritten complaint filed in federal court, Ortiz-Vite named Trump and White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Steven Cheung as defendants.He argued that Trump repeatedly highlighted his case while campaigning on illegal immigration, calling him "America's problem" and featuring his mugshot in campaign advertisements alongside references to "murderers, rapists and drug traffickers.""I took full responsibility for my actions, but for them to use my case for political gain on TV was unjust. Humiliating," Ortiz-Vite wrote in the lawsuit.He said the publicity led to ridicule from prison staff and fellow inmates, adding that he felt stripped of his dignity and reduced to his race and immigration status.Ortiz-Vite also claimed his attorneys warned him that the case had become "high-profile" because of the national attention. "My life was now in the eyes of the public... I was now labeled a cold-blooded murderer in the eyes of the people of this nation," he wrote.According to court records, Ortiz-Vite entered the US illegally and later received protection under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) programme.His DACA status expired in 2019. After a 2020 drunken driving arrest, he was deported to Mexico but later re-entered the US illegally. It remains unclear when he returned.The lawsuit does not identify any specific legal violations, instead arguing that Trump improperly used his case as an example of the Biden administration's immigration policies. Along with monetary damages and a public apology, Ortiz-Vite asked the court to grant him "naturalization to this beautiful country."Legal experts say the case is unlikely to succeed.Matthew Borgula, a former federal prosecutor, said prisoner lawsuits undergo an initial screening and this complaint is unlikely to survive. "The statements were substantially true, and being publicly embarrassed by a politician isn't a constitutional violation. This case should end before it begins," he said.Former Michigan Republican gubernatorial candidate Tudor Dixon also criticised the lawsuit, saying attention should remain on Ruby Garcia rather than "her killer."
Article Summary: Brandon Ortiz-Vite, 27, is serving 39–102 years for killing girlfriend Ruby Garcia. He is seeking $75 million in damages, a public apology, and even US citizenship. He claims the president unfairly turned him into a political symbol during the 2024 election campaign.

Article Title: 'Failed, inhumane policy': Baloch activist raises alarm over spike in student disappearances in region

A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events and alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions.In a statement posted on X, Baloch described the development as alarming and a part of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances that has persisted in the restive province."The cycle of enforced disappearances in Balochistan has never truly stopped, but over the past few days in particular, there has been an alarmingly dangerous surge in the enforced disappearances of students," she said in a statement posted on X.The activist alleged that the disappearances were being justified as part of counter-insurgency operations, but argued that the approach had failed to bring peace to the restive province. Instead, she said, decades of such policies had deepened resentment and contributed to a cycle of unrest and violence."Abducting unarmed and innocent students, as well as young people affiliated with peaceful political organizations, from their homes, hostels, and educational institutions and forcibly making them disappear, and then justifying this oppression in the name of counter-insurgency, is a failed and inhumane state policy that has been imposed on Balochistan for decades," Baloch said, "If this approach were truly a means to bring peace, Balochistan would not be drowning today in this quagmire of blood, unrest, and hatred; rather, the reality is that this policy is not fostering peace but giving birth to even more hatred and violence.Baloch further alleged that young people were being held for years without being charged or brought before a court, and subjected to torture, humiliation and other forms of mistreatment. She argued that such treatment could itself fuel anger and a desire for revenge among those affected."When young people are held for years in state torture chambers without any crime or judicial process, subjected to inhuman violence, humiliation, and torment, it is the state itself that nurtures feelings of revenge and hatred against it through its own policies," she said.According to Baloch, when some of those who later reappear eventually turn to armed violence, state propaganda campaigns focus on those who speak out against enforced disappearances rather than examining the circumstances that may have contributed to the radicalisation of young people.She accused authorities of attempting to make the issue of enforced disappearances controversial by blaming peaceful political activists and human rights defenders for allegedly inciting people or recruiting them for armed groups.Baloch argued that the underlying causes of the continuing conflict were instead "illegal actions, state repression, and tyrannical policies", which she said continued to fuel hostility towards the state.She urged the authorities to review what she described as failed, unconstitutional and oppressive policies, and questioned why decades of alleged repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and collective punishment had failed to establish lasting peace in Balochistan."Instead of offloading the burden of its failed, unconstitutional, and oppressive policies onto the shoulders of the oppressed people and political and human rights activists, the state should ask itself why, despite decades of repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and collective punishments, peace could not be established in Balochistan."The Pakistani government has previously rejected allegations of systematic enforced disappearances, maintaining that its security operations are conducted in accordance with the law and are aimed at combating militancy and maintaining public order.
Article Summary: A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events. She alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions. Article Title: HIV outbreak in Pakistan: How deadly safety lapses at Sindh hospital put children at risk
Article Text:
The SHCC's regulatory inspection found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins, hospital staff could not explain disposal of needles (Photo credit: ANI)

At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures at a state-run hospital.Findings at the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution (SESSI)-run Valika Hospital in Karachi's SITE area revealed needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC), which conducted a regulatory inspection of the state-run hospital, found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins. That hospital staff could not explain where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of."This raised serious concerns about the hospital's medical waste management practices, as it was unclear where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of," the healthcare commission said.The findings came after a major HIV outbreak at the hospital infected 78 children and led to the screening of more than 10,500 people living in the surrounding area.A further 120 people tested positive for HIV, while six deaths have been reported, according to Dawn.Independent inquiries into the outbreak found widespread failures in infection-prevention practices, including the dangerous reuse of single-use syringes. The findings have raised fresh questions over the safety of medical procedures and the handling of infectious waste at one of Sindh's state-run hospitals.During its inspection, the SHCC found that technical personnel were unable to tell inspectors how contaminated medical waste was being disposed of. The hospital had also failed to provide formal safety training to staff or produce written guidelines for handling medical waste and following infection-control procedures.The condition of the hospital's autoclave, a machine used to sterilise medical equipment, could not be verified. Nursing staff and operation theatre personnel were also absent from their posts during duty hours, making it difficult for inspectors to assess routine infection-control practices."The working condition of the autoclave could not be verified during the visit. Nursing and operation theatre (OT) staffs were also not available during duty time, which was making it difficult to assess routine infection control practices of their duty places," the regulatory body added.The SHCC also found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to infection prevention and control guidelines. Hospital staff had poor knowledge of safe medical waste handling, while the private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of the waste had not received proper training."The team found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to IPC guidelines. Staff showed poor knowledge about safe medical waste handling. The private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of medical waste had also not received proper training."The hospital's infection-control failures persisted despite the establishment of an Infection Prevention and Control Committee. The commission also cited staff unionisation and a lack of cooperation with safety protocols as factors that had compromised the handling of medical waste.Following independent inquiries, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah ordered the suspension of 37 officers and officials, including administrators, laboratory personnel and nursing staff.The outbreak has renewed concerns over repeated failures in Pakistan's healthcare system. The country has faced several HIV outbreaks over the past decade, including the 2019 Ratodero outbreak, in which hundreds of children were infected. That investigation also exposed unsafe injection practices, poor sterilisation and weak oversight.The Sindh government has continued screening people in the affected area, promised treatment at public expense and announced a long-term fund for children affected by the outbreak. However, the Valika Hospital findings have raised concerns that similar infection-control failures could exist in other public and private healthcare facilities.
Article Summary: At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi. The outbreak is linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures. Inspectors found needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.

Article Title: Pakistan's fifth province? Gilgit-Baltistan assembly passes key resolution amid PoK unrest
Article Text:
Gilgit-Baltistan (AP photo)

Is Pakistan preparing to make Gilgit-Baltistan its fifth province? Amid ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, the Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, a move that could majorly redefine its administrative structure.The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly on Thursday passed a resolution, backed by both ruling and opposition sides, urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, according to Dawn.The resolution, moved by lawmaker Jalal Ali Shah, also sought constitutional and political rights for the people of the mountainous region.Gilgit-Baltistan, located in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, currently has a semi-provincial administrative status.Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit-Baltistan would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.
Article Summary: The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status. Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.

Article Title: 'Take off uniform and contest elections': Pakistani MP's open challenge to its military
Article Text:
Pakistani MP challenges their military ( Image quality improved using AI)

Critique on Baloch and Pashtun region

Critique of military

Petition filed against Fazl over remarks

Pakistani politician and chief of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl, Maulana Fazlur Rehman, delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government, accusing them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan while warning that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood.""The country is falling apart. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa today, there is no government. After the sun sets in the west, until the sun rises in the morning, the police do not step out of their stations. And if the police do not come out of their stations, then the streets will be handed over to armed groups, then the streets and roads will be at the mercy of bandits," Fazl said during a rally Punjab, Pakistan.He directly addressed the military: "I know your authority in my province — you have no government. You are just sitting inside your grand bungalows in the capitals, legs crossed, thinking you are the rulers. At the very least, in my province, you have no government."Fazl said Balochistan had already slipped out of government control and the Pashtun region was now following suit. "In Balochistan, in the Baloch areas, there were rebellions; the entire Baloch region had slipped out of Pakistan's control. Even today, there is no writ of the Pakistan government there.But we were holding back the Baloch region; now the Pashtun region too is drowning in blood."He described the human toll: "In the Pashtun region, within two or three days, we have received more than fifty bodies. All we did in the markets was buy shrouds for our loved ones. All we did was perform funerals for our loved ones."Fazl took aim at military personnel, accusing them of failing to protect citizens despite being paid from public taxes. "Your youth who are becoming martyrs — they have tied the uniform for this very reason, they are taking their salary for this very reason — that they have to fight for the country's security. What favor are you doing me by throwing your blood on me? You are taking your salary from the taxes of my blood and sweat for precisely this. "He added: "I have taken no salary; I will not form any army. You will leave, but you are pushing my homeland toward personal vendettas for generations to come, pushing it toward murder and plunder forever and ever. Explain this politics to someone else; don't try to explain it to us."Fazl challenged the military to enter politics directly. "If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish."A petition was filed in a court against Fazl over his remarks, with the petitioner arguing that the speech hurt the sentiments of the general public and caused distress to the families of martyrs. The court sought a reply from the National Counter Terrorism Authority by August 17.Pakistani defence minister Khawaja Asif expressed disappointment, calling Fazl's words "unfair." Pakistan’s planning minister Ahsan Iqbal posted on X: "To describe such an unparalleled sacrifice as merely a compensation for a salary is neither fair, nor in accordance with the demands of ethics, and nor aligned with Islamic teachings."
Article Summary: Pakistani politician Maulana Fazlur Rehman delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government. He accused them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. He warned that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood"

Article Title: 'Extreme brutality': Pakistan's PTI to launch nationwide protests for Imran Khan's release
Article Text:

The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf parliamentary party has decided to launch a nationwide movement from August 5 for the release of party chief Imran Khan and acceptance of other demands, a day that will mark the completion of the former prime minister's third year in prison.The decision was made at a meeting chaired by party's interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad, where PTI lawmakers discussed parliamentary affairs and the party's strategy going forward.PTI General Secretary Salman Akram Raja told Dawn that the movement would include public meetings, demonstrations and a long march. "It was also decided that Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas's opinions will be sought for finalising the protest plans and other activities," he said.At a press conference, Gohar said the meeting discussed the health of Imran Khan and his spouse Bushra Bibi. He said August 5 would mark the completion of three years of the PTI founder's imprisonment and rallies would be held across the country to mark the occasion.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023 after an Islamabad trial court found him guilty of corrupt practices in the Tosha Khana case. He has since been convicted in several cases and remains in solitary confinement at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.Raja alleged that Khan had been kept in solitary confinement for months and that no one from his family or lawyers had been allowed to meet him since December last year. "He is not given proper medical care nor is he getting justice from the courts. The oppression and injustice in the country must come to an end," he said.He also warned the government not to launch a crackdown against party workers."Extreme brutality is being carried out here. Imran Khan is being denied meetings with his lawyers, while his sisters are also being barred from seeing him," Raja said as he sat surrounded by party workers outside the jail.Every week, Khan's sisters, lawyers and party workers gather outside Adiala Jail to press the government to allow the family to meet him. On June 14, Khan was taken to a hospital in Islamabad for treatment of his ailing right eye and later shifted back to prison.In a separate development, PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry submitted a list of six leaders to the Adiala jail administration for a meeting with Imran Khan. The list includes Haji Amanullah Awan, Muhammad Shahid Ali Chahan, Syed Hamid Ihsan, Sajjad Ali Butt, Noman Mughal and Aqsa Hayyat Lali.
Article Summary: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf parliamentary party has decided to launch a nationwide movement from August 5. The decision was made at a meeting chaired by party's interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan. Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023 after an Islamabad trial court found him guilty of corrupt practices. He has since been convicted in several cases and remains in solitary confinement at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.
